strengths: FALCON addresses a relevant continual segmentation problem by combining class-imbalance mitigation, preservation of old-class prototypes, and multiple unknown-class clusters. Transferring learned cluster-assignment rules to future classes is a useful methodological direction. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-01/reviews/b03/review-experiment-ngiojlxf/call-930e0d269814470f874a46b5b79257df/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

The evaluation is substantial: three datasets, several incremental schedules, and both convolutional and transformer segmentation models. Table 6 reports improvements over FairCL on ADE20K 100-50 and 100-10: 37.0 to 37.9 and 34.7 to 36.4 mIoU with DeepLab-V3, and 37.6 to 41.9 and 35.5 to 40.3 with transformers.

The loss ablation provides meaningful evidence of improved minority-class accuracy. On ADE20K 100-50, Table 1 raises minority mIoU from 26.4 to 30.8 while also improving majority mIoU from 51.5 to 52.1. Thus, the reduced group disparity does not come from sacrificing majority performance.

Several experiments help substantiate the design. Adaptive visual grammar outperforms its fixed counterpart in Table 2; Table 5 shows initial-class mIoU declining only from 44.9 to 44.4 over six steps. Supplementary studies examine cluster margins, neighborhood sizes, and backbone choices.
weaknesses: The central fairness argument does not establish its claimed geometric mechanism. Propositions 1–2 characterize optimal normalized probabilities, but the conclusion that smaller probabilities imply more compact clusters does not follow: the value 1/L changes with the number of positive samples even when their geometry is unchanged. Consequently, the analysis does not prove that the proposed adjustment remedies minority-cluster dispersion. Separately, Appendix Section 9 invokes a triangle inequality without establishing that the actual contrastive objective is a metric, leaving the claimed distillation upper bound unsupported.

The stated optimization leaves a consequential inconsistency. Equation (8) regularizes distances between prototypes, but Sections 3.1 and 7 describe prototypes as frozen or periodically updated by momentum. No differentiable dependence on the optimized network parameters is specified; under those updates, the regularizer contributes no network gradient. This makes its reported 1.5- and 1.3-point gains in Table 4 difficult to reconcile with the algorithm. Proposition 2 also requires the transition vector to participate in the softmax normalizer, which Equation (4) does not explicitly specify.

The unknown-class ablation does not cleanly isolate attention-based assignment. Section 4.2 states that removing visual grammar also reduces the number of unknown clusters to one, changing two mechanisms simultaneously. A clearly specified comparison retaining multiple unknown clusters with nearest-cluster assignment is needed to attribute the benefit. This distinction matters because the attention architecture explicitly adopts Clusformer [42], and Figure 6 supplies qualitative rather than quantitative assignment evidence.

Reproducibility is incomplete despite the supplied optimizer and prototype-update settings. The manuscript does not adequately specify DBSCAN parameters, feature normalization, visual-grammar pretraining and training schedules, or resolution of competing cluster assignments. Runtime and memory measurements are also absent, so the efficiency claim is not substantiated for the additional transformer, clustering, and feature-extraction stages.

The broad empirical improvements make this a credible contribution near the acceptance boundary. However, the unresolved objective specification and unsupported central theoretical interpretation prevent a confident acceptance recommendation. These concerns carry substantially more weight than correctable presentation errors such as the VOC-style column labels in the ADE20K portion of Table 3.
